title: DeFi
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/0/body: On a **DEX**, you trade straight from **your own wallet**, and no company holds your assets. Instead of an order book, most DEXs use an **automated market maker (AMM)**: a **pool** holding two tokens, where a formula sets the price.
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/1/body: In the most common AMM model, **the product of the two token balances stays constant**. The price comes from the **ratio of the balances**: a pool with 10 ETH and 30,000 USDC puts ETH at about $3,000. When someone buys ETH, the pool's ETH shrinks and **its price goes up**.
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/2/prompt: A pool holds 50 ETH and 100,000 USDC. What's the price of ETH in this pool?
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/2/explanation: Price comes from the ratio of the balances: 100,000 ÷ 50 = $2,000 per ETH.
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/3/statement: In an AMM, when someone buys a token from the pool, that token's price in the pool goes up.
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/3/explanation: The buyer takes that token out of the pool and puts the other one in. The bought token gets scarcer, and the formula pushes its price up.
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/4/body: The bigger your order compared with the **pool size**, the more the price moves (**price impact**). In that same 10 ETH pool, buying with 3,000 USDC gets you about **0.91 ETH**, not 1 ETH. That's why DEXs have a **slippage tolerance**.
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/4/tip: A very high slippage tolerance leaves the door open for "sandwich" bots (MEV) to profit off your trade.
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/5/prompt: Which DEX trade has the lowest price impact?
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/5/options/0: A $1,000 buy from a $10 million pool
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/5/explanation: Price impact depends on your order's size relative to the pool's depth. $1,000 in a $10 million pool is only 0.01% of the pool; the other options are a much bigger share.
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/6/pairs/0/meani: Trade from your own wallet, no middleman
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/6/pairs/1/meani: Prices set by a formula, not an order book
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/6/pairs/2/meani: How much your own order moves the price
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/6/pairs/3/meani: The worst price change you'll accept
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/7/prompt: You want to buy a token on a DEX, and the site warns that the price impact is 18%. What's the best response?
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/7/options/0: Trade smaller or buy from a deeper pool
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/7/options/1: Set slippage to 50% so it's sure to fill
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/7/options/2: Buy with the full amount now, before everyone else
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/7/options/3: Ignore the warning; the number is just for show
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/7/explanation: 18% price impact means you pay about 18% more than the current price the moment you buy. A smaller order or a deeper pool cuts that cost.
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/8/sentence: In an AMM pool, the ___ of the two token balances sets the price, not the ___.
lessons/defi-u2-l1/steps/8/explanation: Each token's price in the pool is the other token's balance divided by its own. There's no order book involved.
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/0/body: Anyone can put two tokens of **equal value** into a pool and become a **liquidity provider (LP)**. In return, you earn a share of the **swap fees** (like 0.3% of each trade) and get an **LP token** as a receipt for your share.
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/1/prompt: Where does a liquidity provider's main income come from?
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/1/options/0: A share of the fees from swaps in the pool
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/1/options/1: Interest paid by a centralized exchange
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/1/options/2: A guaranteed rise in both tokens' prices
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/1/explanation: Every swap has a small fee that's split among LPs according to their share. Token prices come with no guarantee at all.
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/2/body: When one token's price changes, **arbitrageurs** bring the pool back in line with the market, and your share automatically ends up with **less of the token that rose** and **more of the token that fell**. The result: your share is worth less than if you had just **held (HODL)**.
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/3/statement: Impermanent loss only happens when a token's price goes down.
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/3/explanation: Any price change, up or down, causes it. A price that doubles and a price that halves both mean about 5.7% impermanent loss.
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/4/body: The size of impermanent loss depends on **how much** the price changes, not which way. If prices return to where they started, the loss drops back to **zero**; that's why it's called "impermanent". If you exit at the new price, it becomes **permanent**.
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/5/prompt: You put 1 ETH and 2,000 USDC (ETH = $2,000) into a pool. ETH's price quadruples. Roughly what's your share in the pool worth (ignoring fees)?
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/5/explanation: The pool now gives you back about 0.5 ETH and 4,000 USDC: 4,000 + 4,000 = $8,000, which is 20% less than HODL. You're still up from your original $4,000, just less than if you'd simply held.
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/6/prompt: You added liquidity to an ETH/USDC pool at $2,000 (blue line), and now the price has hit 4,000. Roughly what's your impermanent loss compared with HODL?
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/6/explanation: Price has exactly doubled, and impermanent loss for a 2x move is about 5.7%. 20% is for a 4x move. If the fees you've collected are bigger than that, you're still ahead of HODL.
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/7/pairs/0/meani: Someone who deposited two tokens in a pool
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/7/pairs/1/meani: Receipt for your share of the pool
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/7/pairs/2/meani: Falling behind HODL as prices change
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/7/pairs/3/meani: Profit from price gaps between markets
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/8/prompt: Assuming equal fees, which pool probably has the lowest impermanent loss?
lessons/defi-u2-l2/steps/8/explanation: Impermanent loss comes from two token prices drifting apart. Two stablecoins usually both sit near $1, unless one depegs. Memecoins are the opposite: wild swings and high impermanent loss.
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/0/body: On **Proof of Stake** networks, you can **stake** your coins (or delegate them to a validator) and earn a share of the **block validation rewards**. Some networks have an **unbonding period** before you can withdraw, and if the validator misbehaves, part of the stake can get **slashed**.
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/1/body: **APR** is the simple yearly return; **APY** also counts the effect of **compounding** (earning on your earnings). So at the same base rate, APY always shows equal to or higher than APR. When you compare two offers, check which one you're looking at.
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/2/prompt: You staked $2,000 of coins at 6% APR (no compounding). If the coin's price doesn't change, how much reward do you get after one year?
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/2/explanation: 6% of $2,000 = $120. Simple interest means the rewards weren't restaked.
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/3/statement: Staking rewards are usually paid in the coin itself, so if the coin's price falls 30%, you can lose money in dollar terms even with a 10% reward.
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/3/explanation: You have 10% more coins, but each coin is 30% cheaper: 1.1 × 0.7 = 0.77, so about a 23% loss in dollars. Rewards don't protect you from price risk.
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/4/title: Where does the yield come from?
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/4/body: Always ask **where the yield comes from**: trading fees, interest from borrowers, network rewards, or **printing new tokens**. If the yield comes mostly from printing tokens, that token's price usually comes under selling pressure. APYs of **thousands of percent** are usually unsustainable, or a red flag.
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/4/tip: If you don't know where the yield comes from, it's probably coming out of your own pocket.
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/5/pairs/2/meani: Waiting for staked coins to be released
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/5/pairs/3/meani: Moving funds between protocols for yield
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/6/prompt: Which source of yield is more sustainable?
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/6/options/0: Real swap fees from a high-volume pool
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/6/options/1: Nonstop printing of a useless reward token
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/6/options/2: New depositors' money paid out to old ones
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/6/options/3: A stranger's promise of fixed daily profit
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/6/explanation: Real fees come from real demand. Printing tokens dilutes value, and paying old investors with new investors' money is the very definition of a Ponzi scheme.
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/7/sentence: If a protocol's yield comes mostly from ___ new tokens, that token's price usually comes under ___ pressure.
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/7/explanation: Farmers usually sell their reward tokens. Heavy, nonstop supply drags the price down and shrinks the yield in dollar terms too.
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/8/prompt: You have two yield offers in front of you. Which take makes more sense?
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/8/facts/1/value: 2,500% APY · from token printing · anonymous team
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/8/options/0: A is lower risk; B's yield is likely unsustainable and risky
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/8/options/1: B is better because it pays hundreds of times more
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/8/options/2: Both carry the exact same risk, since both are DeFi
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/8/options/3: A is risk-free because it's audited
lessons/defi-u2-l3/steps/8/explanation: B's yield comes from printing tokens, and the team is anonymous: it risks both a price crash and a scam. A makes more sense, but an audit doesn't bring contract risk to zero either.
